title: Texas Mayor Joins Growing Push Against H-1B Use by Public Entities
excerpt: League City Mayor Nick Long says no public entity should use the H-1B program, adding to pressure on taxpayer-funded institutions in a state that already froze new visa petitions through May 2027.
body:
• League City Mayor Nick Long said "no public entity should be using the H-1B program" and that "taxpayers should get taxpayer-funded jobs," responding to Texas State University's filing for a PR specialist role
  • Governor Abbott froze new H-1B petitions at all Texas state agencies and public universities in January 2026, requiring written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission through May 2027
  • Texas public universities sponsor roughly 1,200 H-1B visa holders, with UT Southwestern Medical Center (228), Texas A&M (214), and MD Anderson (171) among the largest users
  • Indians make up an estimated 71% of all approved H-1B applications nationally, making the Texas restrictions directly relevant to the diaspora community

Mayor's Public Opposition

Nick Long, the Republican mayor of League City, Texas, has publicly opposed the use of H-1B visas by public entities, adding a local voice to the growing political pressure on the program in the state.

Long's comments came in response to a post on X announcing that Texas State University had filed a notice of intent to sponsor an H-1B visa for a Public Relations Specialist position. Scott Bowen, the Republican nominee for the Texas House of Representatives, shared the filing and questioned whether none of the university's own communications graduates were qualified for the role.

Long quoted Bowen's post and wrote: "No public entity should be using H-1B program. Taxpayers should get taxpayer funded jobs."

The exchange highlights a growing sentiment among Texas Republican officials that taxpayer-funded institutions should prioritize local hiring, particularly for roles that do not require highly specialized technical expertise. Public universities are cap-exempt under the Immigration and Nationality Act, meaning they can sponsor H-1B workers year-round without participating in the annual lottery — a provision critics argue removes a built-in check on the program's use.

Abbott's Statewide Freeze

Long's comments build on a broader statewide action. In January 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered all state agencies and public universities to immediately halt new H-1B visa petitions, citing "recent reports of abuse in the federal H-1B visa programme."

The freeze applies to agencies controlled by gubernatorial appointees and public universities, and is scheduled to remain in effect until May 31, 2027. Exceptions are possible only with written authorization from the Texas Workforce Commission. Abbott also required affected institutions to submit detailed reports on their H-1B usage, including the number of visa holders, job titles, countries of origin, and visa expiration dates.

"State government must lead by example and ensure that employment opportunities, particularly those funded with taxpayer dollars, are filled by Texans first."

— Greg Abbott, Governor of Texas

Impact on Universities and Medical Centers

Texas public universities collectively sponsor roughly 1,200 H-1B visa holders. The institutions with the largest numbers include the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas with 228 holders, Texas A&M University in College Station with 214, the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston with 171, the University of Texas at Austin with 169, and Texas Tech University in Lubbock with 143.

The College Station metropolitan area, home to Texas A&M, has one of the highest concentrations of H-1B workers in the country at roughly seven approvals per 100 workers, according to Pew Research Center data. Texas A&M's broader system had approximately 1,400 H-1B approvals since 2020 and spent $3.25 million on visa-related costs.

Medical research facilities are particularly vulnerable. About 58% of postdoctoral researchers in science, engineering, and health fields in the US were working on temporary visas as of 2023. The Texas Medical Association has been working to secure clarifications to ensure medical schools and health science centers can continue accessing the program, with a portal now available for requesting exceptions through the Texas Workforce Commission.

Broader Context

The Texas restrictions exist alongside significant federal changes to the H-1B program. The Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B applications in September 2025, replacing the previous random lottery with an income-weighted selection system that prioritizes higher-paid applicants. Legislation has been introduced in Congress — the H-1Bs for Physicians and the Healthcare Workforce Act (H.R. 7961) — to exempt medical professionals from the new fee.

Immigration attorneys have warned that the combined effect of state and federal restrictions could push skilled workers to other states or countries. "The people will have to go home, or have to leave or find a job in another state," said Faye Kolly, an Austin immigration attorney. "Our best state institutions, universities, will have trouble recruiting people, because they can just go elsewhere."

Indians make up approximately 71% of all approved H-1B applications in recent years, according to US Citizenship and Immigration Services data, with technology, engineering, medicine, and research among the primary fields. Among the top 25 Texas employers of H-1B workers, state entities including universities accounted for only about 5% of the total. The majority went to private-sector companies including Cognizant Technology Solutions, which has 3,172 H-1B visas in the state, along with Oracle and Tesla.
